title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Scheduling, Profiling & Ops Playbook
author: Jordan Lee
body:
Purpose and scope
This document consolidates the serving runtime reference material for the eng-serving-runtime team: architecture overview, kernel scheduling policies, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite guidance, recent release notes, known issues, operational runbooks, and team wiki guidance. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and release owners.

1) Executive summary
- Redwood's serving runtime is a high-throughput, GPU-optimized inference engine designed to support multi-tenant hosted, dedicated and private deployments.
- Key goals: predictable tail latency (P99), cost-efficient throughput, graceful degradation via model variants and routing, and observable behavior across stacks.

2) Architecture overview
Short intro: This section describes the logical components, data flow, and deployment model for the runtime.

Components:
- Router / Frontend: accept REST/SDK traffic, authentication, per-tenant routing rules, rate limiting. Owned by: serving-gateway team.
- Inference Scheduler: groups requests into scheduling units, assigns to worker pools based on kernel profiles and model compatibility. Owned by: runtime-scheduler.
- Worker (Executor): GPU process running the model runtime/kernel stack, manages KV cache, beam state, and sequence-level execution. Owned by: serving-runtime.
- Cache layer: prefix/KV cache for token reuse, edge caching for common prompts.
- Telemetry pipeline: traces, per-token costs, latency heatmaps, and model-level metrics.

Deployment patterns and topology:
- Multi-pool: small-latency optimized pools (low-batch) + high-throughput pools (large-batch).
- Regional failover: primary pool per region + automatic fallback to compatible variants in other regions.
- Private deployments: control plane resides in customer network, runtime workers mirror hosted config.

SLOs and thresholds (runtime targets):
- P50 latency (single-token gen): <= 5 ms for optimized pools
- P95 latency: <= 50 ms for conversational workloads (seq <= 1024)
- P99 latency: <= 200 ms (depends on burst policy and batch windows)
- Availability: 99.95% for Dedicated pools; 99.5% for hosted free-tier
- Cost per 1k tokens: monitored per-model and reported in Console

3) Kernel scheduling design and policies
Design goals:
- Minimize latency tail while preserving GPU utilization.
- Route similar shaped workloads to kernels that maximize throughput for expected sequence lengths and attention patterns.

Scheduling primitives:
- Scheduling window: default 2ms for optimized low-latency pools, 8-20ms for throughput pools.
- Key: request attributes: model_id, max_tokens, prompt_length, customer_tier, prefer_low_latency (bool).
- Kernel profile: precomputed shape -> kernel mapping (vectorized codepaths, fused attention kernels, quantized ops).

Policy table (summary):
- If prefer_low_latency == true -> schedule to low-latency pool, window=2ms, max_batch=8
- If model quantized && seq_len <= 512 -> schedule to quantized-optimized kernels, allow larger batch (max_batch=64)
- For long-context models (seq_len >= 2048) -> use memory-optimized kernels, smaller batch sizes, explicit KV streaming
- Retry/fallback: on kernel OOM -> fall back to lower batch size kernel or CPU offload for partial work

Kernel selection lifecycle:
1) Profile model offline across representative sequence lengths and load shapes.
2) Generate kernel mappings and performance table.
3) Check-in mapping into model-catalog and mark compatible runtime images.

4) Profiling playbook (how to investigate and triage perf regressions)
Preparation:
- Ensure the environment is identical to production (image tag, CUDA/cuDNN driver, kernel build).
- Locate a representative prompt set (use /datasets/profiling/{model}/stable-prompts).

Steps (numbered troubleshooting runbook):
1) Reproduce: run a controlled local benchmark using the bench tool: ./bin/runtime-bench --model <model> --shape <seq> --concurrency <n> --image <tag>
2) Capture traces: enable tracing flags (--trace-span --trace-kernel) and collect per-stage timings (load model, init kernels, first-token, per-token).
3) Compare with baseline: compare with last-good trace stored in artifacts (artifacts/runtime/profiles/<model>/<baseline_id>).
4) Identify delta: common deltas are kernel cache warm-up, cublas allocation stalls, unexpected spill to host memory, network serialization delays.
5) Remediation options:
   - Kernel cache warm-up: preheat by sending lightweight warmup requests during startup (see preheat policy).
   - CUBLAS allocation stalls: ensure workspace sizes are consistent; upgrade CUDA driver if indicated; tighten allocator configs.
   - Host spill / GPU OOM: lower batch size, enable quantized kernels, increase per-worker memory reservations.
6) Validate: re-run bench and trace to ensure metrics return to baseline.
7) Postmortem: open a ticket, attach traces, and update the model-catalog performance entry.

Common profiling commands and output parsing:
- ./bin/runtime-bench --model gptx-3b --shape 512 --concurrency 16 --image v2027-02-28
- Output fields to inspect: first_token_ms, per_token_ms_p50/p95/p99, gpu_util_pct, alud_wait_ms, memcpy_ms
- Trace storage: s3://redwood-runtimes/profiles/<model>/<date>/trace.json

5) Benchmarking suite and release gating
Bench goals:
- Automated PR-level smoke tests (functional correctness, small perf check).
- Nightly full-suite (per-model shape matrix across GPU types).
- Canaries and staged rollout performance verification with production traffic shadowing.

Benchmark matrix example (table-as-list):
- GPUs: a100-40g, a100-80g, h100-80g, rtx-6000
- Models: gptx-1b, gptx-3b, seq256/512/1024/2048 shapes
- Metrics: throughput_tokens_per_sec, p50/p95/p99 per-token, memory_peak_mb, tail_oom_count

Acceptance criteria for releases:
- No regression > 10% p50 or > 15% p95 for any core workload compared to baseline
- No new OOMs in nightly suite
- Kernel compatibility verified for each enabled quantization profile

CI integration and artifacts:
- Bench jobs produce artifact bundle (bench.json, flame graphs, traces) uploaded to artifacts/storage with release tag.
- Gating step in pipeline stops promotion if acceptance criteria fail.

6) Release notes (recent highlights)
- 2027-02-28: runtime v2027-02-28
  - Added fused rotary attention kernel for long context models (up to 4096) reducing per-token latency by ~18% on rtx/h100 family.
  - New kernel allocator reduces cublas stalls experienced on mixed tenancy hosts.
- 2026-11-10: runtime v2026-11-10
  - Quantized int8 kernels added for gptx-3b family; default quantized path enabled for dedicated low-cost pools.

7) Known issues (and mitigations)
- Issue: intermittent P99 spikes during autoscaling events
  - Symptom: sudden spike in buffer allocation time and increase in memcpy.
  - Root cause: new worker initialization concurrently warming kernel caches while traffic routes to pool.
  - Mitigation: enable preheat policy with staged warmup (see runbook step 2) and prefer draining connections from older workers first.
- Issue: GPU memory fragmentation causing early OOMs on long-running hosts
  - Mitigation: periodic worker restart policy (weekly rolling restart) and use of per-worker memory compaction on idle.
- Issue: Incorrect quantized kernel results for specific prompt shapes (rare)
  - Mitigation: fallback to FP16 kernel if checksum mismatch detected; add failing prompt to model-catalog test set.

8) Runtime runbooks (operational procedures)
A: Incident: High tail latency (P99 > target)
1) Pager triggers to runtime-oncall.
2) Check service health dashboards (p99 by model, by pool, by region).
3) Identify whether spike is single-model, pool-wide, or multi-region.
4) If single-model: temporarily route traffic to lower-latency variant or increase pool capacity.
5) If pool-wide: scale up low-latency pool and enable spillover routing.
6) If due to new deployment: roll back to previous runtime image.
7) Document timeline and open postmortem if outage > 15 minutes or SLO breached.

B: Incident: Worker OOMs or repeated kernel failures
1) Isolate failing host and disable routing to it.
2) Collect kernel logs and trace bundle (s3 path).
3) If reproducible, adjust max_batch or kernel selection policy for the model.
4) If not reproducible, schedule a repro with same image and hardware; consider driver downgrade as last resort.

C: Routine maintenance (weekly)
1) Validate nightly bench results; look for regressions.
2) Rotate worker images in small batches with preheat enabled.
3) Ensure telemetry retention and indices are healthy.

9) Team wiki and onboarding checklist
- Read this consolidated playbook.
- Run the local bench tooling and submit your first benchmark artifact.
- Join #runtime-ops and subscribe to oncall rota.
- Review model-catalog entries and tagging conventions.

10) Appendix: useful commands, configs and example snippets
- Kernel profile generation (offline): ./scripts/profile_model.sh --model gptx-3b --shapes 256,512,1024 --out profiles/gptx-3b.json
- Example scheduler config (YAML snippet):
  scheduler: 
    low_latency_pool:
      scheduling_window_ms: 2
      max_batch_size: 8
      prefer_low_latency: true
    throughput_pool:
      scheduling_window_ms: 12
      max_batch_size: 64
      allow_quantized: true

- Example bench invocation: ./bin/runtime-bench --model gptx-3b --shape 512 --concurrency 32 --artifacts ./artifacts/local-run

11) Owners and contacts
- Runtime product owner: Priya Nair (product-runtime@redwood.ai)
- Runtime engineering lead: Jordan Lee (jordan@redwood.ai)
- Oncall rotation: See #runtime-oncall Slack channel and PagerDuty schedule

12) Change log and maintenance notes
- 2027-03-04: Consolidated playbook published; added new fused rotary attention notes and updated runbook for autoscaling warmup.
- 2026-11-15: Initial draft created after Q4 performance initiative.

If you are modifying scheduling policies or kernel mappings, coordinate with the model-onboarding AND observability teams and attach a bench artifact to the related model-catalog entry.
